headline: Ram Island's Boulders Load with Peanut Bunker, Stripers Working the Seams on the Drop
subhead: Fishers Island Sound is running cool for mid-July — the fish are pressed tight to the rock, and the albies aren't here yet, but the bait says they're coming.
body_markdown:
The peanut bunker showed up in the pockets off Ram Island about ten days ago, and this week they finally pushed thick enough that you can see them nervous over the boulders on a calm morning — that flicker just under the surface, like somebody shook a jar of dimes. When bait gets nervous over rock, something's under it. I've been poling the skiff along the north side of Ram and through the boulder field off Wamphassuc Point at first light, reading the water the way my grandfather taught me to read it off the breakwater sixty years ago — not by what you see on top, but by what the water does when it hits something hard underneath.

The stripers have been there. Not blitzing, not chasing bait into the air, but working the current seams where the ebb wraps around the bigger rocks and drops bait into slack pockets. That's precision water — you're not bombing a cast, you're dropping a fly or a bucktail three feet off a specific boulder and letting it sink on a controlled count before the current sweeps it into the seam. I've had the best of it on the last two hours of the ebb, fishing a half-ounce olive-and-white bucktail with a chunk of white curly-tail trailer, working it slow along bottom in six to nine feet of water. Fly guys have done well on Clouser minnows and small peanut bunker patterns — olive over white, size 1, stripped in short erratic pulls to mimic that nervous bait behavior rather than a straight swim. Fish have run 22 to 28 inches mostly, a few better ones mixed in that we didn't measure because they went right back — this isn't trophy water in July, it's technical water, and that's exactly why I like it.

Water's running cooler than you'd expect for the date. New London's reading in the mid-60s, which is a few degrees behind where we usually sit this time of July, and that cool water is likely why the bass haven't scattered out onto the flats the way they sometimes do by now — they're staying pressed to structure, holding where the current break gives them an ambush point without burning energy in open water. That's good news for a rock guy. When the fish spread thin over sand, it's a numbers game. When they stay tight to boulders, it's a game I can win with a pole and a quiet approach.

Fluke have been steady but not spectacular in the sandy cuts between the boulder fields — the stretch between Ram Island and the Stonington Breakwater channel, and the deeper hole off Esker Point, have both given up keepers in the 18 to 21 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets, 3-inch, on 3/8-ounce jigheads, drifted slow on the last of the incoming. Nothing to write home about, but a legitimate box fish if you put in the drift time and don't rush the retrieve. Black sea bass are doing their job out around the deeper structure off the east end of Fishers Island — jigging bucktails tipped with squid strips in 25 to 35 feet has produced decent numbers, though you're culling through a lot of shorts to find keepers right now.

Blackfish are still off the table with the summer closure in effect, which is fine by me — I'd rather let those boulder-dwellers alone until the fall run anyway, when the water cools and they pile back onto the structure I've been fishing my whole life.

Now, the question everybody's been asking me at the dock: where are the albies? Honest answer — not here yet, and I wouldn't tell you otherwise. Mid-July is early for Fishers Island Sound. The real run doesn't usually light up until late August into September, when the bay anchovies and silversides get thick in the rips off Watch Hill and around the east end of Fishers. What I am seeing is the forage building the way it should — peanut bunker in the shallows now, and I expect silversides to follow within a couple weeks as the water continues to warm through the back half of July. Squid have been showing in numbers up around Rhode Island Sound and toward Nantucket, and when that squid bite pushes closer to our water it usually means the whole system is loading up for the fall pattern. It's early signal, not a bite report — but it's the kind of thing that tells you to keep your 9-weight rigged and ready.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working the same program: last two hours of the ebb through the Ram Island and Wamphassuc boulder fields for stripers, working current seams tight to structure rather than open water. If we get a stretch of settled southwest wind under 10 knots, I'll be poling the skiff through the shallower boulder pockets on the last of the outgoing, since calm conditions let you actually see the bait and place a cast with precision instead of guessing. If the wind kicks up out of the east, I'd shift to the deeper structure off Fishers Island for sea bass and fluke instead of fighting a chop over the rocks — that's not a day to be running a lower unit through boulder country anyway. The bite this week has been honest work — no giveaways, but consistent enough that a patient angler willing to read the rock instead of the chart is going home with fish.
